summary:
Satellites orbiting the Earth at low altitudes gradually descend due to friction with the upper layers of the atmosphere. The challenge is that maintaining an artificial satellite in a orbit—to prevent it from burning up in the atmosphere—consumes a finite resource, such as rocket fuel . Because of this limitation, the operational lifespan of artificial satellites is significantly restricted.
The concept behind my project involves placing solenoids on a satellite. By supplying the coils with current generated by solar panels, a magnetic field is created that interacts with Earth’s magnetic field; this generates a repulsive force capable of pushing the satellite into a higher orbit.
My initial hypothesis was confirmed using an experimental setup: when current is passed through a solenoid (representing a satellite equipped with a coil), it is repelled away from the "Earth"—a globe containing a magnet that simulates Earth’s magnetic field. However, a challenge arises: the planet’s magnetic field can not only repel the satellite but also rotate it and pull it toward the planet. Applying current to one of them can result in repulsion rather than rotation of the satellite. Multiple solenoids on the satellite make it possible to maintain a fixed orientation through the controlled distribution of current among several electromagnets, which will immediately return the satellite to the desired position whenever it rotates.
details:
The goal of the project is to extend the operational lifespan of satellites in low Earth orbits.

The objective of the project is to develop a method for maintaining a satellite in a designated orbit without the consumption of propellant.

The object of study is the orbital motion of artificial Earth satellites in low orbits.

The subject of study is a method for orbital correction that does not require the consumption of propellant, along with a functional prototype demonstrating its viability.

Relevance: The need to consume propellant for orbital maintenance significantly shortens the operational lifespan of satellites.

Novelty: It has been experimentally confirmed, using a prototype, that a satellite's orbit can be altered without the consumption of propellant.

A Global Problem

Satellites in low Earth orbits lose speed due to friction with the upper layers of the atmosphere and descend toward the Earth's surface.

Existing Solution

Onboard fuel reserves allow a satellite to maintain its designated orbit for a certain period; however, this supply—even when serving as the propellant for an ion thruster—eventually runs out, causing the satellite to descend toward the Earth's surface.

Proposal

Solenoids (Fig. 2), powered by solar panels, generate their own magnetic field, which interacts with the Earth's magnetic field (Fig. 1). This creates a repulsive force that lifts the satellite into a higher orbit (Fig. 3).

Local Problem

A magnetic field is capable of repelling another magnet (Fig. 4) or an electromagnet (Fig. 5)—or rotating it—and then immediately attracting it to its surface.

Hint

Consider a self-balancing scooter —it lacks static equilibrium entirely; however, continuous dynamic "steering" via its wheels allows it to effectively keep a person in an upright position, whether standing still or in motion.

Hypothesis

If several electromagnets are positioned at various angles relative to the Earth's magnetic field and the currents flowing through them are controlled, it is possible to generate a repulsive force without causing the structure to rotate

How it works

An array of several electromagnets oriented in different directions allows for maintaining them in a specific position relative to the main magnetic field through the redistribution of currents (Figs. 6, 7) — a concept verified using an experimental demonstration setup (Figs. 8).

Conclusion

The hypothesis was fully confirmed: the method for extending the orbital lifespan of artificial Earth satellites—devised during the project—will make it possible to significantly increase the time satellites spend in low orbits, utilizing solely the energy of the Sun and the Earth's magnetic field.
